prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

However, the scores of valence and arousal were only similar for videos depicting painted bike lanes in arterial roads and mixed traffic environments on local roads. When comparing arterial roads with painted bike lanes and arterial roads without dedicated cycling infrastructure, results consistently showed that the latter was perceived as less pleasant and more tense. Nevertheless, these findings suggest that riders’ perceived affect (valence and arousal) when riding on arterial roads with painted bike lanes is approx- imately equal to their experience on local roads without dedicated cycling infrastructure. This mirrors past findings which have suggested that riders’ route choices are influenced by perceived safety rather than the presence of dedicated infrastructure (Winters et al., 2011). People referred to a range of issues in the built environment that contributed to feelings of discomfort and anxiety: this included road crossings that were difficult to navigate, a lack of audible signals, poor street lighting, and street furniture and parked SOCIAL & CULTURAL GEOGRAPHY 169 cars that presented obstacles. Robert (VI), for example, explained his anxiety around road crossings: It’s making sure all the audible signals work to let me know when it’s safe to cross. Like there’s a lot around the city that don’t work, so before I get there I’m like God, I hope there’s someone around that I can ask to cross because it makes me feel really nervous. Participants who were Deaf or hard of hearing described the fear of being taken by surprise by cars coming up behind them in street spaces, while some people who used wheelchairs described feeling unsafe as they had to travel on the road due to inaccessible pavements. Marian (MI), who lived in a small flat in a busy inner city area marked by socio- economic deprivation, described how inaccessibility led to her experiencing verbal abuse when out in her wheelchair: ‘Like when I’m on the road, yeah, I’d get beeps – “You f***ing – ” you know what I mean? – “You dope” – there’s a lot of places where I can’t get up on paths’. People with VI also described feelings of insecurity that could result from disorientating aspects of the physical environment. Highlighting the significance of walls as physical markers to assist with navigation, for example, many people discussed the difficulties of navigating large shopping centres and open spaces. As Deirdre who lives alone in a city centre and uses a guide dog, said, ‘I steer clear of plazas because to me they are just massive areas with no sense of knowing where I am’. While some participants described avoiding large shopping centres, for others they were a space of comfort and security. Aoife described her local shopping centre as a safe space because it is was enclosed and easy to navigate in her wheelchair. She articulated access not just in terms of physical environment – the ability of a café or restaurant to accommodate her wheelchair, for example, – but also by affectual encounters of welcome by staff. Robert similarly described this experience of welcome, stating, ‘There’s a bar we go to and they know a few of us in there. So they say ‘Oh your particular spot is not free . . . we’ll bring you down to the end of the bar where there’s a seat’. Particpants’ narratives demonstrate the interconnections that exist between the mate- riality of environments, objects and bodies, to create moments of comfort, but also of anxiety for disabled people as they navigate everyday spaces. These interconnections become particularly visible in the following account from Martin of navigating the streetscape near his home with his white cane. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

],

"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],

"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"
],

"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",
"Appropriate greenery embellishments enhance visual appeal"
],
"comfort": [
"Sparse tree coverage and lack of shading facilities may lead to thermal discomfort in hot weather",
"Lack of benches or resting points reduces comfort for elderly pedestrians",
"Wide, flat sidewalk surfaces support comfortable walking",
"Low traffic noise provides good acoustic comfort"
],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",
"Frequent crossings and curb ramps improve route connectivity",
"Street-level shade and frontage activity increase walking comfort and attractiveness"
]
}
}

1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.
4. Do not mention RAG, retrieval, or prompt instructions in the explanations.

The potential for these conflicts is greatly reduced or eliminated with separated bike lanes that separate bicycle and motor traffic, which may explain why separated bike lanes significantly improve bicyclist comfort and safety above painted bike lanes (McNeil et al., 2015) and are overwhelmingly preferred by bicyclists over painted bike lanes (Aziz et al., 2018; Hardinghaus & Papantoniou, 2020; Ma´rquez & Soto, 2021; Rossetti et al., 2019). However, the scores of valence and arousal were only similar for videos depicting painted bike lanes in arterial roads and mixed traffic environments on local roads. When comparing arterial roads with painted bike lanes and arterial roads without dedicated cycling infrastructure, results consistently showed that the latter was perceived as less pleasant and more tense. Nevertheless, these findings suggest that riders’ perceived affect (valence and arousal) when riding on arterial roads with painted bike lanes is approx- imately equal to their experience on local roads without dedicated cycling infrastructure. This mirrors past findings which have suggested that riders’ route choices are influenced by perceived safety rather than the presence of dedicated infrastructure (Winters et al., 2011). Local roads and streets may therefore provide an untapped opportunity for expanding low-stress bicycling networks without the need to build dedicated bike lanes, particularly if traffic calming measures (e.g., one-way roads, reducing speed limits) are implemented to keep traffic volumes and speeds low. People referred to a range of issues in the built environment that contributed to feelings of discomfort and anxiety: this included road crossings that were difficult to navigate, a lack of audible signals, poor street lighting, and street furniture and parked SOCIAL & CULTURAL GEOGRAPHY 169 cars that presented obstacles. Robert (VI), for example, explained his anxiety around road crossings: It’s making sure all the audible signals work to let me know when it’s safe to cross. Like there’s a lot around the city that don’t work, so before I get there I’m like God, I hope there’s someone around that I can ask to cross because it makes me feel really nervous. Participants who were Deaf or hard of hearing described the fear of being taken by surprise by cars coming up behind them in street spaces, while some people who used wheelchairs described feeling unsafe as they had to travel on the road due to inaccessible pavements. Marian (MI), who lived in a small flat in a busy inner city area marked by socio- economic deprivation, described how inaccessibility led to her experiencing verbal abuse when out in her wheelchair: ‘Like when I’m on the road, yeah, I’d get beeps – “You f***ing – ” you know what I mean? – “You dope” – there’s a lot of places where I can’t get up on paths’. People with VI also described feelings of insecurity that could result from disorientating aspects of the physical environment. Highlighting the significance of walls as physical markers to assist with navigation, for example, many people discussed the difficulties of navigating large shopping centres and open spaces. As Deirdre who lives alone in a city centre and uses a guide dog, said, ‘I steer clear of plazas because to me they are just massive areas with no sense of knowing where I am’. While some participants described avoiding large shopping centres, for others they were a space of comfort and security. Aoife described her local shopping centre as a safe space because it is was enclosed and easy to navigate in her wheelchair. She articulated access not just in terms of physical environment – the ability of a café or restaurant to accommodate her wheelchair, for example, – but also by affectual encounters of welcome by staff. Robert similarly described this experience of welcome, stating, ‘There’s a bar we go to and they know a few of us in there. So they say ‘Oh your particular spot is not free . . . we’ll bring you down to the end of the bar where there’s a seat’. Particpants’ narratives demonstrate the interconnections that exist between the mate- riality of environments, objects and bodies, to create moments of comfort, but also of anxiety for disabled people as they navigate everyday spaces.
